q: A program secretly gathers information about a user's activities, such as the websites she visits, and sends it to someone else without her knowledge. This program is:
x: Spyware is malware that secretly collects information about the user and passes it on. A firewall and antivirus are protection tools, and freeware is simply software that is free to use.

q: A virus is hidden in the small automated commands stored inside a word-processor document, and it runs when the document is opened. This is a:
x: A macro virus lives in a document's macros and runs when the document is opened. A boot sector virus infects the start-up area of a disk, not a document.

q: Why should the virus definitions of an antivirus program be updated regularly?
o: So that newly discovered viruses can be recognised
So that the computer starts up faster
So that forgotten passwords are reset
So that more space is free on the hard disk
x: Antivirus software spots viruses by comparing files with a list of known virus signatures, so new viruses are missed until the list is updated. Updating does not speed up start-up or free disk space.

q: A Caesar cipher shifts every letter of the 26-letter English alphabet forward by the same number of places. Ignoring a shift of 0, how many different keys (shifts) can it have?
x: Shifts of 1 to 25 each give a different cipher; a shift of 26 brings every letter back to itself, the same as shift 0. So there are only 25 useful keys, which is why a Caesar cipher is easy to break by trying them all.

q: In symmetric encryption, how are the encryption and decryption keys related?
o: A public key encrypts and a private key decrypts
No key is used, only a secret method
Each letter of the message has its own public key
The same secret key is used for both
x: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key to encrypt and to decrypt. A public key paired with a private key describes asymmetric (public-key) encryption.

q: Converting an encrypted, unreadable message back into its original readable form is called:
x: Decryption turns ciphertext back into plaintext using the key. Encryption is the opposite step, turning plaintext into ciphertext.

q: A mobile banking PIN has 4 digits, and each digit can be any of 0 to 9. How many different PINs are possible?
x: Each of the 4 places has 10 choices, so 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10 000 PINs (0000 to 9999). The answer 9 999 forgets that 0000 is also a PIN.

q: An antivirus program finds a suspicious file and moves it to a protected area where it cannot run or harm other files, without deleting it yet. This action is called:
x: Quarantine isolates a suspected file so it cannot run, while keeping it in case it turns out to be safe. Formatting would erase the whole disk, and defragmentation only rearranges file pieces.

q: When Ali logs in, the system checks his username and password to confirm that he really is Ali. This step is called:
x: Authentication proves who a user is, for example with a password. Authorisation comes after it and decides what the logged-in user is allowed to do.

q: Which statement is true of a computer virus but NOT of a worm?
o: It is a type of malware
It can damage or delete data
It can spread from one computer to another
It must attach itself to a host file or program to spread
x: A virus needs a host file or program to travel in, while a worm copies itself on its own across a network. Being malware, damaging data and spreading between computers are true of both.

q: Sana's antivirus is fully up to date, yet she types her bank password into a fake website after clicking a link in a phishing e-mail. Why did the antivirus not prevent this?
o: Antivirus software works only when the computer is offline
Phishing tricks the user into giving data, so no harmful program needs to run
Phishing e-mails can be read only after they are decrypted
An updated antivirus deletes every e-mail that has a link
x: Phishing is a trick played on the person: Sana typed her password herself, so there was no virus for the antivirus to find. Antivirus also works online and does not delete every e-mail with a link.

q: A website changes its PIN rule from 4 digits to 6 digits, each digit 0 to 9. By how many times does the number of possible PINs increase?
x: 4 digits give 10⁴ = 10 000 PINs and 6 digits give 10⁶ = 1 000 000, and 1 000 000 ÷ 10 000 = 100. Two extra digits multiply the count by 10 each, not add 2.

q: Software that may be used free of charge for as long as one likes, while its author keeps the copyright and does not share the source code, is called:
x: Freeware is free to use with no time limit, but it stays copyrighted and closed. Shareware is free only for a trial, open-source shares its code, and public domain work has no copyright.

q: Copyright, patents and trademarks are all forms of:
x: Intellectual property rights protect creations of the mind; copyright, patents and trademarks are its main forms. They are legal rights, not crimes or security methods.

q: Software owned by a company that keeps its source code secret and sells licences that let people use it is called:
x: Proprietary (closed-source) software is owned by its maker, whose code stays secret, and users pay for a licence. Freeware is also closed but free, while open-source and public domain software are not kept secret.

q: A student quotes two short lines from a copyrighted book, with the book's name, in a review he writes for the school magazine. This limited use, generally allowed by law, is called:
x: Fair use lets people use small parts of a copyrighted work for purposes such as review, teaching or criticism. It is not plagiarism because the source is named.

q: Small text files that a website stores on a user's computer to remember her visits and settings, and which can also be used to track her browsing, are called:
x: Cookies are small files saved by websites; they are useful for settings but raise privacy concerns because they can track a user across visits. They are not programs that spread like viruses.

q: Someone removes the copy protection from a paid program so that it runs without a valid licence key. This is called:
x: Cracking defeats a program's licence protection and is a form of software piracy. Debugging means finding and fixing errors in one's own code.

q: A bank hires a security expert who, with the bank's written permission, tries to break into its network to find weak points before criminals do. This is:
x: Ethical hacking (penetration testing) is done with the owner's permission to find and fix weaknesses. The same actions without permission would be unauthorised access, a crime.

q: Which of these is personal data that an organisation must protect?
o: The number of computers in a lab
The average mark of a whole class
The opening time of a library
x: A CNIC number identifies one particular person, so it is personal data protected by privacy rules. A class average or a lab's computer count does not identify anyone.

q: An employee copies his company's customer list onto a USB drive so that he can sell it to a rival firm. What is this?
x: Taking an organisation's data without permission to sell it is data theft. A backup is made for the owner's use, not to give data to others.

q: Which pairing of a legal protection with what it protects is correct?
o: Patent – the text of a novel
Copyright – the source code of a program
Copyright – a new method of making a medicine
x: Program code is a written work, so copyright protects it. A novel's text is copyright, a new engine design or medicine-making method is protected by a patent, and a trademark protects brand names and logos.

q: Which statement about open-source software is correct?
o: Its authors still hold the copyright, and its licence sets the conditions for sharing it
It is always in the public domain, with no copyright at all
Nobody is allowed to change its source code
It must always be paid for before it is used
x: Open-source programs are copyrighted works released under a licence that allows studying, changing and sharing under stated conditions. Public domain work, by contrast, has no copyright holder.

q: Hira writes a program and posts its code on her blog. She does not register it anywhere and writes no copyright notice. Who holds the copyright in the code?
o: Nobody, because the code was never registered
Hira, because copyright arises automatically when a work is created
Anyone who downloads the code from the blog
The company that runs the blog website
x: Copyright belongs to the author from the moment an original work is created; registration and notices are optional. Posting it online does not hand the rights to readers or to the blog host.

q: In one region, far fewer women than men own a mobile phone or use the Internet. This situation is an example of:
x: The digital divide is a gap in access to computers and the Internet between groups, here between women and men. Algorithmic bias is unfair output from a computer system, which is not described here.

q: In a shared online document, a reviewer wants to give feedback on a sentence without changing the text itself. What should she add?
x: A comment attaches a note to the selected text for collaborators to read and reply to, leaving the text unchanged. A footnote becomes part of the document's printed content.

q: Group members edit a shared report, and the owner wants every change marked so that she can accept or reject each one. Which feature should they use?
x: Track changes, called suggesting mode in some programs, marks each edit for the owner to accept or reject. Version history only lets earlier copies be viewed or restored, not single changes approved.

q: Where should a backup of important files be kept so that it is still safe if the house suffers a fire or a theft?
o: In another folder on the same laptop
On a second partition of the same hard disk
In a different place, such as cloud storage or another building
On a USB drive kept next to the laptop
x: A backup must be kept away from the original, off-site or in the cloud, so one disaster cannot destroy both. Another folder, partition or a USB next to the laptop would be lost along with it.

q: A program stores all of a user's different strong passwords in encrypted form, unlocked by one master password. Such a program is a:
x: A password manager keeps many strong, unique passwords safely so the user need remember only one. A keylogger is malware that steals passwords rather than protecting them.

q: In computing, bias means that a system:
o: Fails to start because of a hardware fault
Copies itself from one file to another
Gives results that are unfair to certain groups of people
Uses more memory than it needs
x: Bias in computing is when a system's outputs consistently favour or harm some groups, often because of its data or design. Copying itself between files describes a virus, not bias.

q: Before typing card details into a shopping website, which sign shows that the connection to the site is encrypted?
o: The site has many colourful pictures
The address begins with https:// and shows a padlock
x: https and the padlock mean data between the browser and the site is encrypted. A site's pictures, speed or a .com ending say nothing about encryption.

q: A teacher posts the link to her online class meeting publicly on social media. What is the main risk?
o: The video quality of the meeting improves
The link stops working at once
Strangers may join the meeting and disturb the class
x: Anyone who sees a public link can join, so outsiders may enter and disrupt the class; meeting links should be shared only with the students. Posting a link does not change video quality or cancel the meeting.

q: What is the safest place to download a new app for a smartphone?
o: A link received in an unknown SMS
A pop-up advertisement on a website
A file shared by an unknown chat group member
x: Official app stores check apps before listing them, so the risk of malware is much lower. Links from unknown messages, pop-ups or strangers are common ways to spread malware.

q: A team has built a speech-recognition app. What is the best way to find out whether it is biased?
o: Test it only on the developers' own voices
Measure only its overall accuracy on all recordings
Check how quickly it turns speech into text
Compare its error rates for different groups of speakers
x: Bias shows up as different error rates for different groups, such as accents, ages or genders, so results must be compared group by group. A single overall accuracy can look good while one group gets far worse results.

q: Nida receives a chat message from her friend's account asking her to send money urgently for an emergency. What is the safest thing to do?
o: Send the money, since it came from the friend's account
Reply in the same chat asking the sender to prove who they are
Call the friend on a number she already knows to check first
Forward the message to other friends to warn them
x: If the account was hacked, the attacker controls that chat and can answer any question there, so checking through a separate, known channel is safest. Sending money because the account looks familiar is exactly what the scam relies on.

q: Ayesha posts an embarrassing photo and deletes it one hour later. Why might it still cause her harm?
o: Others may already have saved, captured or shared it
Posts cannot be deleted once they are made
Deleting a post also deletes her account
x: In that hour others may have downloaded, screenshotted or forwarded the photo, so copies can stay online; this is part of a lasting digital footprint. Deleting a post does not make it public or remove the account.
